It is a familiar position for many in higher education. Opposing viewpoints are now routinely declared to be violence. That allows professors and students to rationalize their own act of violence or censorship.

The most vivid example was recently seen at Hunter College, which is part of the CUNY system. Just a week earlier, a professor stopped another âviolentâ display of pro-life views in New York. Professor Renee Overdyke of the State University of New York at AlbanyÂshut down a pro-life displayÂ and then resisted arrest.

At the University of California at Santa Barbara, feminist studies associate professor Mireille Miller Young criminally assaulted pro-life advocates on campus, and later pleaded guilty to the crime. She was defended by faculty and students, including many who said she was âtriggeredâ by a pro-life display and that pro-life advocates were âterroristsâ who did not deserve free speech.

It is that easy. You simply declare opposing views âviolentâ and then you can justify your own violence as a matter of self-defense.

The Colorado controversy does not involve acts of violence over misgendering. Moreover, the guide reflects a deep-felt concern that using someoneâs pronouns incorrectly, even unintentionally, leads to âdysphoria, exclusion and alienation.â There are also some positive recommendations in dealing with these difficult situations.

However, this is a university site and there are countervailing free speech costs to characterizing opposing views on pronouns as violence. We haveÂpreviously discussedÂ how other countries are prosecuting those who âmisgender.â Schools in the United States haveÂpromised disciplinary actionÂ against any misgendering despite some court cases ruling for faculty with opposing views on pronouns. EvenÂpassing out âhe/hisâ candiesÂ can result in a university investigation.

Conservative sites likeÂCampus ReformÂ have reported on the Colorado controversy and sought clarification.

Universities are often presented with difficult countervailing interests. On one hand, it must maintain a welcoming and tolerant environment. On the other hand, it must protect free speech values, including the right to express unpopular views or values.

Colorado students have every right to declare misgendering as violence in their eyes, even if many of us disagree. However, the university has an obligation to clearly establish that such views are not the policy or approach of the university itself.Â  The site states âThis information was created by students, for students. The university supports an inclusive environment.â It should state that âwhile the university supports an inclusive environment, the statements on this site are not official statements or policies of the university.â Otherwise, the university should address the free speech implications of declaring misgendering as a violent act.
